inline.s: [Past and future limits] The past limit refers to the past, and the future limit refers to the future. The Jingying Commentary says: “Conditioned dharmas arise one after another. What precedes is the past limit, and what follows is the future limit.” [Severing past and future limits] To have neither a preceding thought nor a succeeding thought, that is, the state in which not a single thought is born. The Record of the Mirror of the Chan School says:

“Thus the Essentials of the Mind Commentary says: If not a single thought is born, then the past and future limits are severed. The luminescent essence stands alone; self and objects are both as-real, and one arrives directly at the source of mind.”
The Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Source of Chan says:
“Hearing once, one awakens a thousand times and attains the great total-holding; when not a single thought is born, the past and future limits are severed.”
[Ping chen]
Also written “ping chen”: to sink into oblivion.
[When the effort reaches this point, the Buddha-recitation has been practiced aright, sympathetic resonance is established, and it is precisely the time to press on with vigor.]

When the effort reaches this point, the Buddha-recitation has been practiced in accord with the Dharma, and sympathetic resonance is established; it is exactly the time to press on with vigor and to ascend further.

[Its feature is like clouds dispersing from the vast sky, the blue heavens fully revealed, and one directly sees the origin. Fundamentally there is nothing to see; the absence of seeing is true seeing, while any seeing is to follow the sense-dust.]

When one directly sees the intrinsic nature, its feature is like clouds scattering across the vast sky, with the blue heavens fully revealed, and one directly sees the original face. Fundamentally there is nothing to be seen; absence of seeing is the real seeing, while any seeing means the sense-roots grasping the dust.
[Absence of seeing is true seeing] The intrinsic nature is formless; it can only be comprehended by spirit, hence it is said that “absence of seeing is true seeing.” The Diamond Sutra says:
“All conditioned appearances are all false and illusory.”
[Having seeing is to follow the dust] “Having seeing” means the sense-roots grasping the dust, for example the eye-root grasping form-dust or the mind-root grasping dharma-dust.

[Arriving at this point, the colors of the mountains and the sounds of the streams are all the truth of the First Meaning; the cawing of crows and the chatter of magpies are none other than the supreme true vehicle.]

Arriving at this point (having realized the essence), all scenes and objects — the colors of the mountains, the sounds of the streams, the caws of crows, the chirps of magpies — all manifest this absolute and inconceivable state: the colors of the mountains and the sounds of the streams are all the truth of the First Meaning (the true reality of all dharmas); the caws of the crows and the chirps of the magpies all proclaim the Dharma of the supreme true vehicle.
[The truth of the First Meaning] The supreme, unsurpassed truth — the true reality of all dharmas. The Buddha said:

“All dharmas are all false and illusory; where they cease, that is called real, that is called the true reality, that is called the dharma-realm, that is called ultimate wisdom, that is called the truth of the First Meaning, that is called the emptiness of the First Meaning.”
(From the Mahaparinirvana Sutra,
Fascicle Forty.)
[Alive and vibrant, it responds to all dharmas yet abides in none; bright and luminous, it illumines all realms yet is utterly without a single thing.]
Alive and vibrant, it responds to all dharmas yet abides in none of them; bright and luminous, it reflects all realms yet in the mind there is utterly no single thing.
Master Hanshan said:

“If one sees the primordial awareness, then all forms, sounds, goods, and profits are clearly comprehended and no longer stir one. Meeting states and conditions in this way is like a mirror reflecting images — no single thing can move one.”
(From the Collected Wanderings in a Dream,
Instructions for Cao Shiju.)
[Speaking of its function, it is like the rising sun in the east — full and bright, illuminating all.]

Speaking of the function of directly seeing one's intrinsic nature, it is like the sun hanging in the sky: darkness is entirely dispelled, the pitfalls and the paths are clearly distinguished, and goblins and ghosts vanish away unnoticed.
[Pitfalls and passages] The pitfalls and the paths.

[Speaking of its essence, it is like the bright moon setting in the west — pure, clear, still, and extinguished. Luminous and still, still and luminous; both abiding and both vanishing, freed from all opposition and perfectly interfused. It is like snow covering a thousand mountains or the sea swallowing all imagery: only one color, utterly without another flavor, nothing to be attached to, no obstacle, spontaneously at ease.]

Speaking of the essence of the intrinsic nature, it is like the bright moon setting in the west — pure, clear, still, and extinguished. Luminous and still, still and luminous; stillness and luminosity both abide and both vanish, perfectly interfused, freed from all opposition. It is like white snow covering a thousand mountains or the sea swallowing all things: only one color, with nothing of any other flavor; nothing to be attached to, no obstacle, spontaneously at ease.
[Still like the bright moon setting in the west, pure, clear, still, and extinguished] Only when the moon sets is there the ultimate. The Strict Record of the Five Lamps says:
“A monk asked: When the bright moon hangs in the sky, what is that? The master
(Chan Master Caoshan)
replied: He is still a man below the steps. The monk said: I beg you, Master, to raise him up the steps. The master said: When the moon has set, come and see me.”

[Both abiding and both vanishing, freed from opposition and perfectly interfused] From the standpoint of phenomenal characteristics, dharmas arise through conditions, hence stillness and luminosity both abide (both existing); from the standpoint of the essential principle, dharmas are empty in nature, hence stillness and luminosity both vanish (both nonexistent). The existence (both abiding) and the nonexistence (both vanishing) of stillness and luminosity occur at the same time yet without mutual obstruction, freed from all opposition and perfectly interfused. Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:

“Since dependent origination and emptiness of nature occur at the same time, spontaneously there appears the countenance of both vanishing and both abiding. Both vanishing and both abiding, simultaneously without obstruction — that is the upward, interfused, inconceivable truth of the First Meaning.”
(From the Collected Works of Master Chewu,

The Great Meaning of the Two Schools of Prajna and the Pure Land.) [Dependent origination and emptiness of nature] Dependent origination means that all dharmas arise through the union of many conditions; this is spoken from the standpoint of phenomenal characteristics. Emptiness of nature means that the nature of all dharmas is originally empty, not truly existing; this is spoken from the standpoint of the essential principle. [Free from opposition] Free from all opposition; synonymous with “absolute.” [All imagery] All the phenomena of the universe; here it refers to the manifold things in the world.

It is like snow covering a thousand mountains, the sea swallowing all imagery — only one color, utterly without another flavor, nothing to be attached to, no obstacle, spontaneously at ease’ — this is a further vivid explanation of the above: pure, clear, still, and extinguished, stillness and luminosity both abiding and both vanishing, freed from opposition and perfectly interfused.

[As for its benefit: in the present life, though still not free from the Saha world, one constantly joins the ocean-gathering of the lotus assembly; at death, one at once ascends to the highest grade and suddenly realizes the Buddha-vehicle.]

Speaking of the benefit of realizing Buddha-recitation samadhi: in the present life, though still not free from the Saha world, one constantly joins the lotus-pool ocean-gathering of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; at the hour of death, one at once ascends to the highest grade and is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; upon reaching that land one suddenly realizes the Buddha-vehicle and awakens to the patient endurance of non-arising.

[The Buddha-vehicle] The Tathagata uses the One-vehicle teaching of true reality to carry all sentient beings together to the far shore of nirvana; hence it is called the Buddha-vehicle. [Suddenly realizing the Buddha-vehicle] The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says:

“Having been born in that land, one sees the Buddha's physical body with all the marks complete; sees the bodhisattvas with their physical characteristics complete; radiant light and jewelled groves preach the wonderful Dharma. Having heard it, one instantly awakens to the patient endurance of non-arising. In a moment one passes among all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, and before each Buddha receives in succession the prophecy of future enlightenment; returning to that land, one attains countless hundreds of thousands of dharanis. This is called one reborn in the highest grade of the highest class.”

blocks.text: 5. It Is a Matter Within the Family

inline.s: [Only the householder knows the matters of the household; speak of them to the outsider, and slander is certain without doubt.]
Only the householder understands the matters of the household; if one speaks of them to an outsider, one will without any doubt meet with slander.

Master Yinguang was concerned that this passage, which speaks of investigating through Buddha-recitation, might arouse the debate “Is it Chan? Is it the Pure Land school?” So he said with special earnestness: It is not fitting to speak of this to outsiders. For only when one's state has reached this step does one understand its interfusion and finality.
In fact, whether it is the Pure Land practice depends crucially on whether one is complete in faith and vows. Master Ouyi (the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:
“A Chan practitioner who wishes to be born in the West need not change to Buddha-recitation; as long as he is complete in faith and vows, then his contemplating Chan is the Pure Land practice.”
(From the Collected Pure Land Teachings of Master Ouyi,
Casual Talks in the Brahma Chamber.)

Moreover, one who investigates through Buddha-recitation not only is complete in faith and vows, but also has one-minded, undisturbed concentration as a basis; to recite the Buddha's name and to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is naturally the Pure Land practice.

When Buddha-recitation has reached the point of directly seeing the origin, it naturally converges with the upward path of the Chan school, because both are the clarification of the mind and the seeing of the nature; as the saying goes: “There are many gates of skillful means, but to the origin there is not a second road.” The instruction of Chan Master Baizhang, quoted in this passage when describing the state of realizing Buddha-recitation samadhi,

“The spiritual radiance shines alone, entirely detached from the sense-roots and the sense-dust. The essence is revealed as true and eternal, not confined to words. The mind-nature is undefiled, originally complete in itself. But once you depart from false conditions, you are the Thus-come Buddha”
— this is the Chan saying of the bottom of the bucket falling out.
Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:
“Long ago someone asked Master Yunqi
(that is, Master Lianchi, the eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school)

How can contemplation Chan and Buddha-recitation be made to interpenetrate? The master replied: If they were indeed two separate things, then it would be necessary to interpenetrate them. Ah, how profound is this saying! For Chan is the Chan of the Pure Land, and the Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan. They are not two things in the first place; why use interpenetration?”
(From the Collected Works of Master Chewu,

The Great Meaning of the Two Schools of Prajna and the Pure Land.) (Translation: In the past, someone asked Master Lianchi: “How can contemplation Chan and Buddha-recitation be interpenetrated?” The master replied: “If contemplation Chan and Buddha-recitation were indeed two separate things, then interpenetration would be needed.” Ah, this truly explains the essential purport of both contemplation Chan and Buddha-recitation with perfect clarity! Chan is the Chan of the Pure Land; the Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan. They are not two things in the first place; what is there to interpenetrate?)
This passage answers the guest's second question: after realizing Buddha-recitation samadhi, how does one carry on the work of protecting and maintaining?

[Protect and maintain] Protection and spontaneous functioning: these are the two stages of eliminating habitual tendencies after seeing the nature. “Protection” means doing one's utmost to tend the sacred embryo so that it is not harmed. “Spontaneous functioning” means that after the sacred embryo has grown and is capable of protecting itself, one then accords with conditions and functions naturally, further refining oneself amid favorable and adverse conditions in order to accomplish the four patient endurances. To use the analogy of overcoming addiction: the first stage is to keep away from all drugs; this is protection. Once the addiction has been entirely overcome, one must live the life of an ordinary person so that even when the drug is within easy reach, the mind is unmoved. [The four patient endurances] The patient endurance of subjugation, the patient endurance of docility, the patient endurance of non-arising, and the patient endurance of still extinction. The patient endurance of subjugation: for a beginning practitioner who wishes to endure favorable and adverse conditions, he must first subdue and tame his mind. The patient endurance of docility: after the mind has been subdued and tamed for a long time, when encountering states and conditions one can endure naturally without forced restraint; at this time the mind is gentle, compliant, and well-adapted. The patient endurance of non-arising: for those in the sage positions, they realize that all dharmas originally do not arise; sentient and insentient being alike arise through conditions without self-nature and are empty in their very substance. Therefore within this nature-void Dharma the mind of endurance does not move, and one directly realizes non-arising. The patient endurance of still extinction: for the sage at the fruit stage, he fully realizes the still, extinguished realm of nirvana; both the characteristics of motion and stillness accord with Suchness.
[Again the guest asked: In daily life, responding universally to all conditions, how can one's every glance be bodhi and every instance be the Way?]

The guest asked again: In daily life, when responding universally to all conditions, how can one be present in awareness at all times and places, functioning spontaneously with conditions and never departing from the Way?

[Bodhi] Translated into Chinese as “awakening.” [Every glance is bodhi] Whatever the gaze falls upon is all the realm of awakening. [Every instance is the Way] Every matter and every object is the Way. This says that the Way is present everywhere. [Every instance] Every matter, every object.

[Answer: When the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of dharmas cease. The ten thousand realms do not go beyond the one mind, and the one mind interpenetrates the ten thousand realms. If one understands that the mind's essence is originally empty, what harm is there in embracing all imagery?]

I replied: When the mind arises, all manner of states arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of states cease. The ten thousand realms do not go beyond the one mind, and the one mind can interpenetrate the ten thousand realms. If one awakens to the mind's essence being originally empty, what harm is there in embracing all imagery? — For having awakened to the emptiness of the mind's essence, one is truly master of oneself and can interpenetrate the ten thousand realms: within, one is not turned by thoughts; without, one is not drawn by states.

[When the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of dharmas cease] When the mind arises (the first stirring of thought), one enters the dream of ignorance and all manner of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases (the extinction of subtle thought), the dream of ignorance ends and all manner of dharmas cease. Therefore, “mind arising” here means the first stirring of thought, and “mind ceasing” means the extinction of subtle thought. (See the essay
Mind, Self-nature, and Tathagatagarbha
for details.)

[You must know that all imagery is like an illusion; arising and ceasing are only the one mind. All conditions do not bind you; you are originally liberated. The six sense-dusts are not evil; dwell equally with right awakening. Mind and realm are one suchness; what attachment or obstacle is there?]

You must know that the myriad phenomena are like an illusion; their arising and ceasing are only one's own mind — when the mind arises all manner of dharmas arise, and when the mind ceases all manner of dharmas cease. Therefore, all conditions do not bind you; you are originally liberated. The six sense-dusts are not evil; if the mind is not defiled by them and not bound by them, it is the same as the Buddha. As long as the mind remains unmoved in suchness, what obstruction do the dusty realms present?
[You must know that all imagery is like an illusion; arising and ceasing are only the one mind] The Diamond Sutra says:
“All conditioned appearances are all false and illusory.”

The Buddhas, amid the very apparent arising and ceasing, see only non-arising; sentient beings, amid the perfectly still non-arising, see only arising and ceasing. [Right awakening] The Buddha's wisdom. [One suchness] “One” means equal and undivided; “suchness” means constant and unchanging.

[Do you not see the Avatamsaka's realm of phenomena-without-obstruction? As it is said: “In every single mote of dust are all buddha-lands; in every single mind are all minds; each mind and each dust mutually encompass one another, layer upon layer without end, without obstruction.”]

Do you not see the Avatamsaka's realm of phenomena-without-obstruction? As it is said: in every single mote of dust there are all buddha-lands, and in every single mind there are all minds; each mind and each dust mutually pervade one another — dust and lands, minds and minds, layer upon layer without end, without mutual obstruction. Having awakened to the mutual interpenetration of all dharmas, endless and without obstruction, one naturally has every glance be bodhi and every instance the Way.

[The realm of phenomena-without-obstruction] One of the four dharma-realms. [The four dharma-realms] Established by the Avatamsaka school, namely: the realm of phenomena, the realm of principle, the realm of the unimpeded interpenetration of principle and phenomena, and the realm of phenomena-without-obstruction. The differentiated characteristics of the myriad worldly dharmas, each distinct and not to be confused, are called the “realm of phenomena.” The equal essential principle of true suchness, on which all dharmas depend, is called the “realm of principle.” As true suchness can give rise to all dharmas, all dharmas are themselves true suchness; the essential principle and the phenomenal characteristics mutually interfuse and mutually contain, reaching everywhere without obstruction: principle is itself phenomena and phenomena are themselves principle; this is called the “realm of the unimpeded interpenetration of principle and phenomena.” All dharmas mutually interpenetrate, layer upon layer without end, without mutual obstruction; one and many are identical, great and small mutually contain one another; lifting one gathers all, and each is complete and corresponding; this is called the “realm of phenomena-without-obstruction.” [Layer upon layer without end] Speaking in terms of motes and buddha-lands: in every single mote of dust there are all buddha-lands, and in each of those buddha-lands there are countless motes of dust; in each of those motes of dust again there are all buddha-lands. Extending thus, dust contains lands, and lands again contain dust — layer after layer continuing without end; hence it is called “layer upon layer without end.” Likewise, mind and mind, mind and dust, are also like this, layer upon layer without end.

[For this reason, the material realms and the dust on a hair, the cloud-like terraces and the jewelled nets, all proclaim the ocean of intrinsic nature and all expound the true vehicle. Reaching vertically to the limit of the three times and pervading horizontally the ten directions, even a single hair-tip's worth that is not the Way cannot be found. Thus every dharma and every instance is none other than the great stilling-and-extinction ground; every thought and every recollection accords with the ocean of all-knowing wisdom.]

For this reason, the material realms and the dust on a hair, the cloud-like terraces and the jewelled nets, all proclaim the rational nature of true suchness and all expound the true teaching. Reaching vertically to the limit of the three times (past, present, future) and pervading horizontally the ten directions (east, south, west, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, below), even seeking for something as fine as the tip of a hair that is not the Way, one cannot find it. Therefore every dharma and every instance is none other than the great stilling ground of the Way; every thought and every recollection all accord with the Tathagata's all-knowing wisdom.

[The material realm] The realm of material objects and vessels: a general name for the mountains, rivers, great earth, dwellings, and all articles and implements. [Dust on a hair] The fine dust that lodges at the tip of a hair. [Cloud-like terrace] A terrace so lofty it pierces the clouds. [Jewelled net] A net of precious jewels. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life says:
“Rare and wonderful jewelled nets are spread over it.”

[Ocean of intrinsic nature] The rational nature of true suchness, as deep and vast as the ocean. [True vehicle] The true teaching. [Stilling ground] An abbreviation for the stilling-and-extinction ground of the Way. The Collected Annotations on the Four Teachings says:
“Where the abode turns with the Dharma, that is called the stilling ground.”
[Sarvajna] Translated into Chinese as “all-knowing wisdom” — the great wisdom of the Buddha's ultimate, complete, perfect fruit.

[Only mind is the wondrous realm; only realm is the wondrous mind. Departing from the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations, freed from opposition and perfectly interfused — how could one attain it and conceive or speak of it!]
Only mind is the wondrous realm; only realm is the wondrous mind. Departing from and cutting off all thought and speech, absolutely interfused — how could one attain it and then ponder or discuss it!

[Only mind is the wondrous realm; only realm is the wondrous mind] The wondrous realm that is only mind; the wondrous mind that is only realm. The Buddha said: “The mind is not of itself mind; because of realms there is mind. The realm is not of itself realm; because of mind there is realm.” [The four propositions and the hundred negations] This is a common expression used to eradicate sentient beings' deluded clinging to the erroneous views of being and nonbeing, and to make clear the principle that true emptiness is formless and ungraspable; the Chan school often uses it to guide students. [The four propositions] The first: being. The second: nonbeing. The third: both being and nonbeing. The fourth: neither being nor nonbeing. The first proposition, “being,” says that appearances exist, focusing on phenomenal characteristics. The second, “nonbeing,” says that the essence is absent, focusing on the essential principle. The third, “both being and nonbeing,” says appearances exist while the essence is absent, focusing on the whole — phenomenal characteristics and the essential principle. The fourth, “neither being nor nonbeing,” transcends the opposition of being and nonbeing. Seng Zhao (one of the four wise disciples under Master Kumarajiva) said:

“Therefore the sutra says: True prajna is neither being nor nonbeing, neither arising nor ceasing; it cannot be spoken or shown to people. Why? To say that it is not being is to say that it is not that which is being, not that it is merely the absence of being; to say that it is not nonbeing is to say that it is not that which is nonbeing, not that it is merely the absence of nonbeing. Neither being nor not-being, neither nonbeing nor not-nonbeing — thus Subhuti speaks prajna all day long, yet is said to have spoken nothing.”
(From the Treatise of Seng Zhao,

Reply to Liu Yimin.) [The hundred negations] This means a hundred kinds of negation. The hundred negations are an unfolding of the four propositions. Within “being” there are: being as being; being as nonbeing; both being and nonbeing; neither being nor nonbeing. Within “nonbeing” there are likewise four propositions: nonbeing as being; nonbeing as nonbeing; both being and nonbeing; neither being nor nonbeing. So within each proposition there are four propositions — four times four makes sixteen propositions. Within the sixteen, there are sixteen for the past, sixteen for the present, and sixteen for the future, making forty-eight. Already arisen and not yet arisen, each forty-eight, makes ninety-six; then adding the fundamental four — “being,” “nonbeing,” “both being and nonbeing,” and “neither being nor nonbeing” — makes one hundred propositions. [Departing from the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations] This means departing from and cutting off all thought and speech.

[What has been spoken above is like the blind men feeling the elephant: though they had not left the elephant, I feared it was not the whole elephant. Hence I have written it down to submit for the scrutiny of those who have personally seen it.]

What has been said above is like the blind men feeling the elephant: though they had not left the elephant, I feared it was not the whole elephant. Therefore I have written it down to verify it before the wise among you who have personally seen the state of Buddha-recitation samadhi.
Further reading:
On “Who is reciting the Buddha's name?”
